text: Eleven blocks in the cold, and the cold got the better of the eleven blocks.

text: Between two and four there is nobody out but me and whoever is paid to be.
The sky over the river had gone grey along the bottom edge.
Shutters up, gratings back, and a man with a hose putting the night down the drain.
The El went over while I was crossing, and for twenty seconds the street had nothing to say.
A patrolman came the other way and we each decided the other was nobody.
The milk wagon had the whole block ahead of me, iron tyres on the cobbles.
The bells at the corner rang the half hour at my back.
A whistle went off the river, two long and one short, and nobody looked up.
A truck dropped the last edition at the kerb and pulled away with the doors still open.
Chairs were going up on the tables behind me before I had the door shut.
Past the corner, past the grating, past the same two men who had not moved.
The fight card droned on over some radio down the block, and half an hour went with it.
A ball game recap crackled out of a radio somewhere, then went to advertising, then went quiet.
Down at the corner a regular took his stool, same as any night, and the half hour turned.
Somebody's regular seat scraped back at a bar down the block. Another half hour gone.
The beat cop came round again, unhurried, and the half hour went with him.
Somewhere off a block a patrolman's steps went past and faded. Half an hour, gone.
The same four bars came down from the floor above, over and over, and then the half hour was up.
A piano lesson two floors up quit for the night. The half hour went quiet after it.
The El went over, and for twenty seconds nothing else could be heard. Half an hour gone with it.
The El rattled through again, right on its schedule, and time moved with it.
St. Malachy's rang the half hour, same as it always does.
The bells went again somewhere off to the east, marking the half hour plain and clear.
A truck went by dropping the last edition at the corner stand. Half an hour, and the ink still wet.
Somewhere a paper boy was already hawking the late edition. The half hour had gotten away from me.
A fuse went somewhere on the block and a whole row of windows went dark. Half an hour passed in it.
The lights flickered once down the street and held. Another half hour gone.
The rain came on somewhere off to the west, and half an hour went with the first of it.
Rain started up again, thin and steady, and time went with it.
The milk wagon worked its way down the next block, iron tires loud on the stone. Half an hour, gone with it.
A milk wagon's bell sounded somewhere off, right on its usual round. Another half hour behind me.
Somewhere off, a crowd let out of a picture house all at once, loud for a minute and then gone. Half an hour with it.
The last house let out down the avenue, and the street noise came and went with it.
A shift changed over at the garage down the block, engines catching one after another. Half an hour, gone in the noise.
The night men were punching in somewhere close, machinery starting up. Another half hour behind me.
Somebody was singing the same two verses under a window a block over, until a shoe came down and ended it. Half an hour with it.
A drunk was singing off-key somewhere down the street, on and on, and then not.
A dumbwaiter squealed somewhere up a shaft close by. Half an hour, gone in the noise of it.
The dumbwaiter cable groaned again two buildings over, right on its own schedule.
An iceman's wagon worked the block, blocks going in on shoulders. Half an hour went with the delivery.
Ice went into somebody's box down the street, dropped once on the step with a crack. Another half hour gone.
A whistle went off the river, two long and one short. Half an hour, marked and gone.
The river whistle sounded again, carrying a mile inland easy. Time moved with it.
Half an hour gone, and nothing to show for it but sore feet.
I checked my watch twice in the time it took to cross the street.
Another half hour slipped by in the time it took to light a cigarette.
The night had that late feel already, the kind that makes an hour feel longer.
Half an hour slid past somewhere between one block and the next.
I walked it slow, and the half hour walked with me.
Somewhere a door closed for the night, and half an hour went with the sound of it.
The half hour went by quiet, same as most of them do this time of night.
I stood on the corner long enough to lose track, and picked it back up half an hour later.
Half an hour gone, same as the last one, and no closer to anything.
The night was young enough to waste half an hour and not feel it yet.
I let half an hour go by without noticing, which happens less as the night wears on.
The dead hours ran together, and another half hour went with them.
Half an hour passed slow, then all at once, the dead hours running together.
I stood in a doorway out of the wind and lost half an hour to it.
Nothing moved for half an hour but the hands on my watch.
The half hour went by heavy, same as the small hours always do.
I walked the long way around, and it cost me half an hour I didn't have.
Half an hour disappeared somewhere between one cigarette and the next.
The quiet swallowed the half hour whole.
I counted the half hour off against my own tired feet.
Half an hour gone in the worst stretch of the night, and nothing in it.
The city held its breath for half an hour, and so did I.
Half an hour went by with nothing in it worth writing down.
The sky was starting to think about morning, and half an hour went with the thought.
Half an hour passed while the dark thinned out, degree by degree.
The night was running out, and half an hour of it went with these steps.
I felt the half hour more than I tracked it, an ache settling behind my eyes.
Half an hour gone, and the first gray was showing over the rooftops.
The morning was still a rumor, but half an hour closer to being true.
I used the half hour walking, which beat standing still and feeling it.
Half an hour went by with the last of the dark.
The night had thinned enough to see the end of it, half an hour off yet.
Half an hour slipped by somewhere in the change of light.
I lost half an hour to the cold, mostly just standing in it.
The half hour went quiet, same as the last ones before dawn.
The morning was up in earnest now, and half an hour went with the traffic's first push.
Half an hour went while the city woke up around it.
I spent the half hour dodging the morning crowd, which was slower going than the empty streets.
The half hour went by loud, for a change, with the day starting up.
Half an hour gone, and the night was somebody else's problem now.
The light was full and flat, and the half hour went with it, ordinary and unremarked.
I felt the whole night catch up with me in that half hour.
Half an hour passed in the noise of the morning shift changing over.
The city had places to be now, and my half hour went along with the rush of it.
Half an hour gone, and I could have used the sleep more than the progress.
The morning traffic ate the half hour without noticing it had.
I let the half hour go by watching the day start, a small mercy after the night I'd had.
